Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Given that $$-1$$ is a root of $$2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+3=0$$, find the two positive roots.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Use the known root to factor out $$(x+1)$$ and then solve the remaining quadratic factor.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Because $$-1$$ is a root, $$f(-1)=0$$ and $$(x+1)$$ is a factor of $$2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+3$$. Divide $$2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+3$$ by $$(x+1)$$: Step 1: $$\frac{2x^{3}}{x}=2x^{2}$$, so $$2x^{2}(x+1)=2x^{3}+2x^{2}$$ and subtract to get $$-7x^{2}-4x+3$$; Step 2: $$\frac{-7x^{2}}{x}=-7x$$, so $$-7x(x+1)=-7x^{2}-7x$$ and subtract to get $$3x+3$$; Step 3: $$\frac{3x}{x}=3$$, so $$3(x+1)=3x+3$$ and the remainder is $$0$$. Thus $$2x^{3}-5x^{2}-4x+3=(x+1)(2x^{2}-7x+3)$$. Solve $$2x^{2}-7x+3=0$$: discriminant $$\Delta=(-7)^{2}-4\cdot2\cdot3=49-24=25$$, so $$x=\dfrac{7\pm5}{4}=\dfrac{12}{4},\dfrac{2}{4}=3,\dfrac12$$. The two positive roots are $$x=3$$ and $$x=\dfrac12$$.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that $$\dfrac{x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}}\equiv\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}$$ (for $$x\ge0,y\ge0,x\ne y$$).
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Rationalise the denominator by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate $$\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Start with $$\dfrac{x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}}$$ and multiply by $$\dfrac{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}$$: $$\dfrac{x-y}{\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y}}\cdot\dfrac{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}{\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}}=\dfrac{(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}$$. The denominator simplifies using the difference of squares: $$(\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})=x-y$$, so the fraction becomes $$\dfrac{(x-y)(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y})}{x-y}=\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}$$ (since $$x\ne y$$). Hence the identity holds.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Use completing the square to prove that $$n^{2}-8n+20$$ is positive for all values of $$n$$.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Complete the square: $$n^{2}-8n+20=(n^{2}-8n+16)+4=(n-4)^{2}+4$$. For any real $$n$$, $$(n-4)^{2}\ge0$$, so $$(n-4)^{2}+4\ge4>0$$. Therefore $$n^{2}-8n+20$$ is positive for all values of $$n$$.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the quadrilateral $$A(1,1),\ B(3,2),\ C(4,0),\ D(2,-1)$$ is a square.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Use the distance formula to show all four sides have equal length and show that adjacent sides are perpendicular (for example using dot products).
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: First find the side vectors: $$\overrightarrow{AB}=(3-1,2-1)=(2,1)$$, $$\overrightarrow{BC}=(4-3,0-2)=(1,-2)$$, $$\overrightarrow{CD}=(2-4,-1-0)=(-2,-1)$$, $$\overrightarrow{DA}=(1-2,1-(-1))=(-1,2)$$. Their squared lengths are $$|\overrightarrow{AB}|^{2}=2^{2}+1^{2}=5$$, $$|\overrightarrow{BC}|^{2}=1^{2}+(-2)^{2}=5$$, $$|\overrightarrow{CD}|^{2}=(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}=5$$, $$|\overrightarrow{DA}|^{2}=(-1)^{2}+2^{2}=5$$, so all sides are equal. Check perpendicularity: $$\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=2\cdot1+1\cdot(-2)=2-2=0$$, so angle at $$B$$ is a right angle. A quadrilateral with four equal sides and one right angle is a square, so $$ABCD$$ is a square.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_title: Even sum of consecutive odd numbers
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the sum of two consecutive positive odd numbers less than ten gives an even number.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Represent two consecutive odd numbers in algebraic form and add them.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Let the two consecutive positive odd numbers be $$2n+1$$ and $$2n+3$$, where $$n$$ is an integer and $$2n+3<10$$. Their sum is $$(2n+1)+(2n+3)=4n+4=4(n+1)$$, which is a multiple of $$4$$ and therefore even. Hence the sum of any two consecutive positive odd numbers (and in particular those less than ten) is an even number.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the statement “$$n^{2}-n+3$$ is a prime number for all values of $$n$$” is untrue.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Take $$n=4$$. Then $$n^{2}-n+3=4^{2}-4+3=16-4+3=15$$. But $$15=3\times5$$ is not prime. So there exists at least one value of $$n$$ for which $$n^{2}-n+3$$ is not a prime number, and the statement “for all values of $$n$$” is therefore untrue.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that $$(x-\frac{1}{x})(x^{\frac{4}{3}}+x^{-\frac{2}{3}})\equiv x^{\frac{1}{3}}\!\left(x^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right).$$
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Expand the left-hand side using distributive law and simplify using index laws $$x^{a}x^{b}=x^{a+b}$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Start with $$(x-\frac{1}{x})(x^{\frac{4}{3}}+x^{-\frac{2}{3}})=x\cdot x^{\frac{4}{3}}+x\cdot x^{-\frac{2}{3}}-\frac{1}{x}\cdot x^{\frac{4}{3}}-\frac{1}{x}\cdot x^{-\frac{2}{3}}.$$ Using index laws, $$x\cdot x^{\frac{4}{3}}=x^{1+\frac{4}{3}}=x^{\frac{7}{3}},\quad x\cdot x^{-\frac{2}{3}}=x^{1-\frac{2}{3}}=x^{\frac{1}{3}},\quad \frac{1}{x}\cdot x^{\frac{4}{3}}=x^{\frac{4}{3}-1}=x^{\frac{1}{3}},\quad \frac{1}{x}\cdot x^{-\frac{2}{3}}=x^{-\frac{2}{3}-1}=x^{-\frac{5}{3}}.$$ Hence the expression becomes $$x^{\frac{7}{3}}+x^{\frac{1}{3}}-x^{\frac{1}{3}}-x^{-\frac{5}{3}}=x^{\frac{7}{3}}-x^{-\frac{5}{3}}$$. Factor out $$x^{\frac{1}{3}}$$: $$x^{\frac{7}{3}}-x^{-\frac{5}{3}}=x^{\frac{1}{3}}\!\left(x^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right).$$ Thus $$(x-\frac{1}{x})(x^{\frac{4}{3}}+x^{-\frac{2}{3}})\equiv x^{\frac{1}{3}}\!\left(x^{2}-\frac{1}{x^{2}}\right).$$

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: The equation $$x^{2}-kx+k=0$$, where $$k$$ is a positive constant, has two equal roots. Prove that $$k=4$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: For a quadratic $$ax^{2}+bx+c=0$$ to have equal roots, its discriminant $$b^{2}-4ac$$ must be zero.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Here $$a=1$$, $$b=-k$$, $$c=k$$. Equal roots give $$b^{2}-4ac=0\Rightarrow(-k)^{2}-4\cdot1\cdot k=0\Rightarrow k^{2}-4k=0\Rightarrow k(k-4)=0$$. Since $$k$$ is positive, $$k\neq0$$, so $$k-4=0\Rightarrow k=4$$. Therefore the only positive value of $$k$$ for which the equation has equal roots is $$k=4$$.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_title: Distance between opposite edges of a regular hexagon
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the distance between opposite edges of a regular hexagon of side length $$\sqrt{3}$$ is a rational value.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Use the fact that a regular hexagon can be divided into six equilateral triangles and relate the distance between opposite edges to the height of one such triangle.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: A regular hexagon of side length $$s$$ can be split into six equilateral triangles each of side $$s$$ with a common centre. The distance between opposite edges (the “flat-to-flat” distance) is twice the apothem (the perpendicular distance from the centre to a side). For an equilateral triangle of side $$s$$, the height (and so the apothem of the hexagon) is $$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s$$. Thus the distance between opposite edges is $$2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s=\sqrt{3}s$$. With $$s=\sqrt{3}$$, this distance is $$\sqrt{3}\cdot\sqrt{3}=3$$, which is a rational number. Hence the distance between opposite edges is rational.

Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_title: Difference of squares of consecutive even numbers
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.question_text: Prove that the difference of the squares of two consecutive even numbers is always divisible by $$4$$.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.hint: Represent consecutive even numbers as $$2n$$ and $$2n+2$$ and subtract their squares.
Chapter 7 - Algebraic methods.correct_answer: Let the two consecutive even numbers be $$2n$$ and $$2n+2$$, where $$n$$ is an integer. Their squares are $$(2n)^{2}=4n^{2}$$ and $$(2n+2)^{2}=4n^{2}+8n+4.$$ The difference (larger minus smaller) is $$(2n+2)^{2}-(2n)^{2}=(4n^{2}+8n+4)-4n^{2}=8n+4=4(2n+1).$$ Since this is a multiple of $$4$$ for every integer $$n$$, the difference of the squares is always divisible by $$4$$.

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_title: Finding a parameter from a coefficient
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: The coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ in the expansion of $$(2+ax)^{3}$$ is $$54$$. Find the possible values of the constant $$a$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Expand $$(2+ax)^{3}$$ using the binomial theorem and read off the $$x^{2}$$ term; then set that coefficient equal to $$54$$ and solve for $$a$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: Using coefficients $$1,3,3,1$$, $$(2+ax)^{3}=8+3\cdot4\cdot ax+3\cdot2\cdot(a x)^{2}+(a x)^{3}=8+12ax+6a^{2}x^{2}+a^{3}x^{3}$$, so the coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ is $$6a^{2}$$; solving $$6a^{2}=54$$ gives $$a^{2}=9$$ and hence $$a=3$$ or $$a=-3$$.

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: The coefficient of $$x^{3}$$ in the expansion of $$(2-x)(3+bx)^{3}$$ is $$45$$. Find the possible values of the constant $$b$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: First expand $$(3+bx)^{3}$$ using coefficients $$1,3,3,1$$, then multiply by $$(2-x)$$ and collect the $$x^{3}$$ term; finally equate that coefficient to $$45$$ to get an equation in $$b$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: We have $$(3+bx)^{3}=27+27bx+9b^{2}x^{2}+b^{3}x^{3}$$. Now $$(2-x)(3+bx)^{3}=2(27+27bx+9b^{2}x^{2}+b^{3}x^{3})-x(27+27bx+9b^{2}x^{2}+b^{3}x^{3})$$. The $$x^{3}$$ terms come from $$2\cdot b^{3}x^{3}$$ and $$-x\cdot9b^{2}x^{2}=-9b^{2}x^{3}$$, so the coefficient of $$x^{3}$$ is $$2b^{3}-9b^{2}$$. Setting this equal to $$45$$ gives $$2b^{3}-9b^{2}-45=0$$; this cubic has one real root, approximately $$b\approx5.30$$, and two complex roots, so the real value of $$b$$ is the real solution of $$2b^{3}-9b^{2}-45=0$$.

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: Work out the coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ in the expansion of $$(p-2x)^{3}$$. Give your answer in terms of $$p$$.

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: Exactly 10 heads in 20 fair tosses has probability $$\left(^{20}C_{10}\right)0.5^{20}$$. Calculate this and describe the likelihood.

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&(1-2x)^{p}=\sum_{r=0}^{p}\binom{p}{r}(-2x)^{r}.\\&\text{For }x^{2}:\ r=2,\ \text{coefficient is }\binom{p}{2}(-2)^{2}=4\binom{p}{2}.\\&\text{Given }4\binom{p}{2}=40\Rightarrow \binom{p}{2}=10.\\&\binom{p}{2}=\frac{p(p-1)}{2}=10\Rightarrow p(p-1)=20\Rightarrow p^{2}-p-20=0.\\&p=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{1+80}}{2}=\frac{1\pm9}{2}\Rightarrow p=5\ \text{or}\ p=-4.\\&\text{Since }p>0,\ p=5.\\&\text{(b) Coefficient of }x:\ r=1,\ \binom{5}{1}(-2)=5\cdot(-2)=-10.\\&\text{(c) Coefficient of }x^{3}:\ r=3,\ \binom{5}{3}(-2)^{3}=10\cdot(-8)=-80.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: a Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of $$x$$, of the binomial expansion of $$(5 + px)^{30}$$, where $$p$$ is a non-zero constant. (2 marks) b Given that in this expansion the coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ is $$29$$ times the coefficient of $$x$$ work out the value of $$p$$. (4 marks)
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: For part (a), use the binomial theorem to write the terms for $$r=0,1,2$$. For part (b), equate the expressions for the coefficients of $$x$$ and $$x^{2}$$ using the condition “coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ is $$29$$ times coefficient of $$x$$”, then solve for $$p$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&(5+px)^{30}=\sum_{r=0}^{30}\binom{30}{r}5^{30-r}(px)^{r}.\\&\text{(a) First three terms (}r=0,1,2\text{) in ascending powers of }x:\\&r=0:\ \binom{30}{0}5^{30}(px)^{0}=5^{30}.\\&r=1:\ \binom{30}{1}5^{29}(px)=30\cdot 5^{29}p x.\\&r=2:\ \binom{30}{2}5^{28}p^{2}x^{2}.\\&\text{So the first three terms are }5^{30}+30\cdot 5^{29}p x+\binom{30}{2}5^{28}p^{2}x^{2}+\cdots.\\&\text{(b) Coefficient of }x:\ C_{1}=30\cdot 5^{29}p.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{2}:\ C_{2}=\binom{30}{2}5^{28}p^{2}.\\&\text{Given }C_{2}=29C_{1}:\\&\binom{30}{2}5^{28}p^{2}=29\cdot 30\cdot 5^{29}p.\\&\text{Since }p\neq0,\ 5^{28}\neq0,\ \text{divide both sides by }5^{28}p:\\&\binom{30}{2}p=29\cdot 30\cdot 5.\\&\binom{30}{2}=\frac{30\cdot 29}{2}=435,\ \text{so }435p=29\cdot 30\cdot 5=4350.\\&p=\frac{4350}{435}=10.\\&\therefore p=10.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: (a) Find the first four terms, in ascending powers of $$x$$, of the binomial expansion of $$(1 + qx)^{10}$$, where $$q$$ is a non-zero constant. (b) Given that in the expansion of $$(1 + qx)^{10}$$ the coefficient of $$x^{3}$$ is $$108$$ times the coefficient of $$x$$, work out the value of $$q$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use the binomial expansion $$(1+qx)^{10}=\sum_{r=0}^{10}\binom{10}{r}(qx)^{r}$$ to find the first four terms. For part (b), write the coefficient of $$x$$ and of $$x^{3}$$ in terms of $$q$$, form the equation “coefficient of $$x^{3}$$ $$=108\times$$ coefficient of $$x$$”, and solve for $$q$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{For }(1+qx)^{10},\ T_{r+1}=\binom{10}{r}(qx)^{r}.\\&\text{First four terms (}r=0,1,2,3\text{):}\\&r=0:\ \binom{10}{0}(qx)^{0}=1.\\&r=1:\ \binom{10}{1}(qx)^{1}=10qx.\\&r=2:\ \binom{10}{2}(qx)^{2}=45q^{2}x^{2}.\\&r=3:\ \binom{10}{3}(qx)^{3}=120q^{3}x^{3}.\\&\text{So the first four terms are }1+10qx+45q^{2}x^{2}+120q^{3}x^{3}+\cdots.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x\text{ is }10q.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{3}\text{ is }120q^{3}.\\&\text{Given }120q^{3}=108\times 10q=1080q,\ \text{with }q\neq0.\\&\Rightarrow 120q^{2}=1080\Rightarrow q^{2}=\frac{1080}{120}=9.\\&\therefore q=\pm 3.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: (a) Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of $$x$$, of the binomial expansion of $$(1 + px)^{11}$$, where $$p$$ is a constant. (b) The first three terms in the same expansion are $$1$$, $$77x$$ and $$qx^{2}$$, where $$q$$ is a constant. Find the value of $$p$$ and the value of $$q$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use $$(1+px)^{11}=\sum_{r=0}^{11}\binom{11}{r}(px)^{r}$$. For part (a), take $$r=0,1,2$$. For part (b), equate the coefficient of $$x$$ to $$77$$ to find $$p$$, then substitute in the coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ to find $$q$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&(1+px)^{11}=\sum_{r=0}^{11}\binom{11}{r}(px)^{r}.\\&\text{First three terms:}\\&r=0:\ \binom{11}{0}(px)^{0}=1.\\&r=1:\ \binom{11}{1}(px)=11px.\\&r=2:\ \binom{11}{2}(px)^{2}=55p^{2}x^{2}.\\&\text{So the first three terms are }1+11px+55p^{2}x^{2}+\cdots.\\&\text{Given that the first three terms are }1,77x,qx^{2}.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x:\ 11p=77\Rightarrow p=7.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{2}:\ 55p^{2}=55\cdot 7^{2}=55\cdot 49=2695.\\&\therefore q=2695.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: (a) Write down the first three terms, in ascending powers of $$x$$, of the binomial expansion of $$(1 + px)^{15}$$, where $$p$$ is a non-zero constant. (b) Given that, in the expansion of $$(1 + px)^{15}$$, the coefficient of $$x$$ is $$(-q)$$ and the coefficient of $$x^{2}$$ is $$5q$$, find the value of $$p$$ and the value of $$q$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use $$(1+px)^{15}=\sum_{r=0}^{15}\binom{15}{r}(px)^{r}$$. For (a) take $$r=0,1,2$$. For (b) express the coefficients of $$x$$ and $$x^{2}$$ in terms of $$p$$, equate them to $$-q$$ and $$5q$$ respectively, then solve the simultaneous equations for $$p$$ and $$q$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&(1+px)^{15}=\sum_{r=0}^{15}\binom{15}{r}(px)^{r}.\\&\text{First three terms:}\\&r=0:\ 1.\\&r=1:\ \binom{15}{1}px=15px.\\&r=2:\ \binom{15}{2}p^{2}x^{2}=105p^{2}x^{2}.\\&\text{So the first three terms are }1+15px+105p^{2}x^{2}+\cdots.\\&\text{Given coefficient of }x\text{ is }-q:\ 15p=-q\Rightarrow q=-15p.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{2}\text{ is }105p^{2},\ \text{given as }5q.\\&\therefore 105p^{2}=5q=5(-15p)=-75p.\\&105p^{2}+75p=0\Rightarrow 15p(7p+5)=0.\\&p\neq0\Rightarrow 7p+5=0\Rightarrow p=-\frac{5}{7}.\\&q=-15p=-15\left(-\frac{5}{7}\right)=\frac{75}{7}.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use the binomial theorem with $A=3$ and $B=-\dfrac{x}{5}$: $\left(3-\dfrac{x}{5}\right)^{10}=\sum_{r=0}^{10}\binom{10}{r}3^{10-r}\left(-\dfrac{x}{5}\right)^{r}$. For (b), set $3-\dfrac{x}{5}=2.98$ to find $x$ and substitute this into the first few terms of the expansion.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{(a)}\ \left(3-\dfrac{x}{5}\right)^{10}=\sum_{r=0}^{10}\binom{10}{r}3^{10-r}\left(-\dfrac{x}{5}\right)^{r}.\\&r=0:\ \binom{10}{0}3^{10}=3^{10}=59049.\\&r=1:\ \binom{10}{1}3^{9}\left(-\dfrac{x}{5}\right)=10\cdot19683\left(-\dfrac{x}{5}\right)=-\dfrac{196830}{5}x=-39366x.\\&r=2:\ \binom{10}{2}3^{8}\left(-\dfrac{x}{5}\right)^{2}=45\cdot6561\cdot\dfrac{x^{2}}{25}=\dfrac{295245}{25}x^{2}=\dfrac{59049}{5}x^{2}.\\&\text{Thus the first three terms are }59049-39366x+\dfrac{59049}{5}x^{2}+\cdots.\\&\text{(b)}\ 2.98^{10}=\left(3-\dfrac{x}{5}\right)^{10}\ \text{when }3-\dfrac{x}{5}=2.98\Rightarrow\dfrac{x}{5}=0.02\Rightarrow x=0.1.\\&\text{To estimate }2.98^{10},\ \text{substitute }x=0.1\text{ into the truncated expansion: }59049-39366(0.1)+\dfrac{59049}{5}(0.1)^{2},\ \text{and evaluate this value as the approximation.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: a Find the first $4$ terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of $(1 - 3x)^{5}$. Give each term in its simplest form. b If $x$ is small, so that $x^{2}$ and higher powers can be ignored, show that $(1 + x)(1 - 3x)^{5} \approx 1 - 14x$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use the binomial theorem $(1+u)^{n}=\sum_{r=0}^{n}\binom{n}{r}u^{r}$ with $u=-3x$ to obtain the first four terms. For the approximation, replace $(1-3x)^{5}$ by its truncated expansion up to the $x$-term and then multiply by $(1+x)$, discarding $x^{2}$ and higher powers at the end.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{(a)}\ (1-3x)^{5}=\sum_{r=0}^{5}\binom{5}{r}(-3x)^{r}=1+5(-3x)+10(-3x)^{2}+10(-3x)^{3}+5(-3x)^{4}+(-3x)^{5}.\\&\qquad=1-15x+90x^{2}-270x^{3}+405x^{4}-243x^{5}.\\&\text{Thus the first four terms in ascending powers of }x\text{ are }1-15x+90x^{2}-270x^{3}.\\&\text{(b)}\ \text{For small }x,\ \text{ignore }x^{2}\text{ and higher in }(1-3x)^{5}:\\&\qquad(1-3x)^{5}\approx1-15x.\\&\text{Then }(1+x)(1-3x)^{5}\approx(1+x)(1-15x)=(1-15x)+x(1-15x).\\&\qquad=1-15x+x-15x^{2}=1-14x-15x^{2}.\\&\text{Ignoring the }x^{2}\text{ term gives }(1+x)(1-3x)^{5}\approx1-14x.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: A microchip company models the probability of having no faulty chips on a single production run as $P(\text{no fault})=(1-p)^{n},\ p<0.001,$ where $p$ is the probability of a single chip being faulty, and $n$ being the total number of chips produced. a State why the model is restricted to small values of $p$. b Given that $n=200$, find an approximate expression for $P(\text{no fault})$ in the form $a+bp+cp^{2}$. c The company wants to achieve a $92\%$ likelihood of having no faulty chips on a production run of $200$ chips. Use your answer to part b to suggest a maximum value of $p$ for this to be the case.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: The approximation in part b uses a truncated binomial expansion of $(1-p)^{n}$, which is only accurate when $p$ is very small so that higher powers of $p$ can be neglected. For part b, expand $(1-p)^{200}$ up to the $p^{2}$ term. For part c, set the approximate expression equal to $0.92$, solve the resulting quadratic equation in $p$, and choose the smaller root (since $p$ must be small and $p<0.001$).
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{(a)}\ \text{The binomial expansion of }(1-p)^{n}\text{ is approximated by keeping only the first few terms in }p.\\&\text{This is only accurate when }p\text{ is very small, so the model is restricted to small }p.\\&\text{(b)}\ P(\text{no fault})=(1-p)^{200}.\\&\text{Using }(1+u)^{n}=1+nu+\tfrac{n(n-1)}{2}u^{2}+\cdots\text{ with }u=-p,\ n=200:\\&(1-p)^{200}\approx1+200(-p)+\tfrac{200\cdot199}{2}(-p)^{2}=1-200p+19900p^{2}.\\&\text{Hence }a=1,\ b=-200,\ c=19900,\ \text{so }P(\text{no fault})\approx1-200p+19900p^{2}.\\&\text{(c)}\ \text{Require }P(\text{no fault})\approx0.92\text{ for }n=200:\\&1-200p+19900p^{2}\approx0.92.\\&\Rightarrow 19900p^{2}-200p+0.08\approx0.\\&\text{Solve }19900p^{2}-200p+0.08=0\text{ using the quadratic formula:}\\&p=\frac{200\pm\sqrt{(-200)^{2}-4\cdot19900\cdot0.08}}{2\cdot19900}=\frac{200\pm\sqrt{40000-6368}}{39800}=\frac{200\pm\sqrt{33632}}{39800}.\\&\sqrt{33632}\approx183.4,\ \text{so }p\approx\frac{200\pm183.4}{39800}.\\&\text{This gives }p\approx\frac{16.6}{39800}\approx4.17\times10^{-4}\ \text{or }p\approx\frac{383.4}{39800}\approx9.63\times10^{-3}.\\&\text{Since }p\text{ must be very small and the model assumes }p<0.001,\ \text{take }p_{\max}\approx4.2\times10^{-4}.\\&\text{Thus a suitable maximum value is }p\approx0.00042.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: The 16th row of Pascal’s triangle is shown below. $$1 \quad 15 \quad 105 \quad \dots \quad \dots$$ a Find the next two values in the row. b Hence find the coefficient of $$x^{3}$$ in the expansion of $$(1 + 2x)^{15}$$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use the fact that the $n$th row (starting with row 0) of Pascal’s triangle consists of the binomial coefficients $$\binom{n}{0},\binom{n}{1},\dots,\binom{n}{n}$$; the 16th row corresponds to $n=15$. Then use the binomial expansion $$(1+2x)^{15}=\sum_{r=0}^{15}\binom{15}{r}(2x)^{r}$$ and pick the $r=3$ term.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{Row 16 corresponds to }n=15,\text{ so its entries are }\binom{15}{0},\binom{15}{1},\binom{15}{2},\dots,\binom{15}{15}.\\&\binom{15}{0}=1,\ \binom{15}{1}=15,\ \binom{15}{2}=105,\ \binom{15}{3}=\dfrac{15\cdot14\cdot13}{3\cdot2\cdot1}=455,\ \binom{15}{4}=\dfrac{15\cdot14\cdot13\cdot12}{4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}=1365.\\&\text{So the next two values in the row are }455\text{ and }1365.\\&\text{For }(1+2x)^{15},\ T_{r+1}=\binom{15}{r}(2x)^{r}.\\&\text{The }x^{3}\text{ term has }r=3:\ T_{4}=\binom{15}{3}(2x)^{3}=\binom{15}{3}2^{3}x^{3}=455\cdot8x^{3}=3640x^{3}.\\&\text{Hence the coefficient of }x^{3}\text{ is }3640.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: The coefficient of $x^{2}$ in the binomial expansion of $(2 + kx)^{8}$, where $k$ is a positive constant, is $2800$. a Use algebra to calculate the value of $k$. b Use your value of $k$ to find the coefficient of $x^{3}$ in the expansion.

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{For }(2+kx)^{8},\ T_{r+1}=\binom{8}{r}2^{8-r}(kx)^{r}.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{2}\ (r=2):\ \binom{8}{2}2^{6}k^{2}=28\cdot64k^{2}=1792k^{2}.\\&1792k^{2}=2800\Rightarrow k^{2}=\frac{2800}{1792}=\frac{25}{16}\Rightarrow k=\frac54\ (\text{since }k>0).\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{3}\ (r=3):\ \binom{8}{3}2^{5}k^{3}=56\cdot32\left(\frac54\right)^{3}.\\&\left(\frac54\right)^{3}=\frac{125}{64},\ 56\cdot32\cdot\frac{125}{64}=56\cdot\frac12\cdot125=28\cdot125=3500.\\&\text{So }k=\frac54\text{ and the coefficient of }x^{3}\text{ is }3500.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: In the binomial expansion of $(2 + px)^{5}$, where $p$ is a constant, the coefficient of $x^{3}$ is $135$. Calculate: a the value of $p$, b the value of the coefficient of $x^{4}$ in the expansion.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use the general term $\binom{5}{r}2^{5-r}(px)^{r}$. For $x^{3}$ take $r=3$ and equate the coefficient to $135$ to find $p$. Then take $r=4$ to obtain the $x^{4}$ coefficient.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&(2+px)^{5}=\sum_{r=0}^{5}\binom{5}{r}2^{5-r}(px)^{r}.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{3}\ (r=3):\ \binom{5}{3}2^{2}p^{3}=10\cdot4p^{3}=40p^{3}.\\&40p^{3}=135\Rightarrow p^{3}=\frac{135}{40}=\frac{27}{8}\Rightarrow p=\frac32.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{4}\ (r=4):\ \binom{5}{4}2^{1}p^{4}=5\cdot2\left(\frac32\right)^{4}=10\cdot\frac{81}{16}=\frac{810}{16}=\frac{405}{8}.\\&\text{So }p=\frac32\text{ and the coefficient of }x^{4}\text{ is }\frac{405}{8}.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: Find the constant term in the expansion of $$\left(\dfrac{x^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{2}{x}\right)^{9}.$$
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Write the general term $\binom{9}{r}\left(\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}\right)^{9-r}\left(-\dfrac{2}{x}\right)^{r}$ and determine the value of $r$ that makes the power of $x$ equal to $0$. Then evaluate the corresponding coefficient.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&T_{r+1}=\binom{9}{r}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)^{9-r}\left(-\frac{2}{x}\right)^{r}=\binom{9}{r}\frac{x^{2(9-r)}}{2^{9-r}}\cdot\frac{(-2)^{r}}{x^{r}}.\\&\text{Power of }x:\ 2(9-r)-r=18-3r.\\&\text{For a constant term }18-3r=0\Rightarrow r=6.\\&T_{7}=\binom{9}{6}\left(\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right)^{3}\left(-\frac{2}{x}\right)^{6}=\binom{9}{6}\frac{x^{6}}{2^{3}}\cdot\frac{64}{x^{6}}=\binom{9}{6}\cdot\frac{64}{8}.\\&\binom{9}{6}=\binom{9}{3}=84,\ \frac{64}{8}=8\Rightarrow \text{constant term}=84\cdot8=672.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: a Find the first three terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of $(2 + px)^{7}$, where $p$ is a constant. The first $3$ terms are $128$, $2240x$ and $qx^{2}$, where $q$ is a constant. b Find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use $(2+px)^{7}=\sum_{r=0}^{7}\binom{7}{r}2^{7-r}(px)^{r}$. List the terms for $r=0,1,2$ to get the first three terms in terms of $p$. Then equate the coefficient of $x$ to $2240$ to find $p$ and substitute back to find $q$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&(2+px)^{7}=\binom{7}{0}2^{7}+\binom{7}{1}2^{6}px+\binom{7}{2}2^{5}p^{2}x^{2}+\cdots\\&=128+7\cdot64px+21\cdot32p^{2}x^{2}+\cdots\\&=128+448px+672p^{2}x^{2}+\cdots.\\&\text{Given the first three terms are }128,\ 2240x,\ qx^{2}.\\&448p=2240\Rightarrow p=\frac{2240}{448}=5.\\&q=672p^{2}=672\cdot25=16800.\\&\text{So }p=5\text{ and }q=16800.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: a Write down the first three terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of $(1 - px)^{12}$, where $p$ is a non-zero constant. b Given that, in the expansion of $(1 - px)^{12}$, the coefficient of $x$ is $q$ and the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $6q$, find the value of $p$ and the value of $q$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use $(1+u)^{12}$ with $u=-px$ to obtain the first three terms. Then identify the coefficients of $x$ and $x^{2}$ in terms of $p$, set them equal to $q$ and $6q$ respectively, and solve the resulting equations for $p$ and $q$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&(1-px)^{12}=1+12(-px)+\binom{12}{2}(-px)^{2}+\cdots=1-12px+66p^{2}x^{2}+\cdots.\\&\text{Thus the first three terms are }1-12px+66p^{2}x^{2}.\\&\text{Given coefficient of }x\text{ is }q:\ q=-12p.\\&\text{Coefficient of }x^{2}\text{ is }66p^{2},\ \text{given as }6q=6(-12p)=-72p.\\&66p^{2}=-72p\Rightarrow p(66p+72)=0.\\&p\neq0\Rightarrow 66p+72=0\Rightarrow p=-\frac{72}{66}=-\frac{12}{11}.\\&q=-12p=-12\left(-\frac{12}{11}\right)=\frac{144}{11}.\\&\text{So }p=-\frac{12}{11}\text{ and }q=\frac{144}{11}.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_title: Binomial expansion of $\left(2+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^{7}$ and estimate for $2.05^{7}$
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: a Find the first $3$ terms, in ascending powers of $x$, of the binomial expansion of $\left(2+\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^{7}$, giving each term in its simplest form. b Explain how you would use your expansion to give an estimate for the value of $2.05^{7}$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use the binomial theorem $(A+B)^{7}=\sum_{r=0}^{7}\binom{7}{r}A^{7-r}B^{r}$ with $A=2$ and $B=\dfrac{x}{2}$, then take $r=0,1,2$ for the first three terms. To estimate $2.05^{7}$, notice that $2.05=2+0.05$ and match $0.05$ with $\dfrac{x}{2}$ to choose $x$, then substitute this value into the truncated expansion.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{(a)}\ \left(2+\frac{x}{2}\right)^{7}=\sum_{r=0}^{7}\binom{7}{r}2^{7-r}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)^{r}=\sum_{r=0}^{7}\binom{7}{r}2^{7-2r}x^{r}.\\&r=0:\ \binom{7}{0}2^{7}=128.\\&r=1:\ \binom{7}{1}2^{5}x=7\cdot32x=224x.\\&r=2:\ \binom{7}{2}2^{3}x^{2}=21\cdot8x^{2}=168x^{2}.\\&\text{Thus the first three terms are }128+224x+168x^{2}+\cdots.\\&\text{(b)}\ 2.05^{7}=(2+0.05)^{7}=\left(2+\frac{x}{2}\right)^{7}\ \text{when }\frac{x}{2}=0.05\Rightarrow x=0.1.\\&\text{Using the first three terms: }2.05^{7}\approx128+224(0.1)+168(0.1)^{2}=128+22.4+1.68=152.08.\\&\text{So we substitute }x=0.1\text{ into }128+224x+168x^{2}\text{ to estimate }2.05^{7}.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.question_text: $g(x)=(4+kx)^{5}$, where $k$ is a constant. Given that the coefficient of $x^{3}$ in the binomial expansion of $g(x)$ is $20$, find the value of $k$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.hint: Use the general term $\binom{5}{r}4^{5-r}(kx)^{r}$ in $(4+kx)^{5}$ and take $r=3$ for the $x^{3}$ term. Equate its coefficient to $20$ and solve for $k$.
Chapter 8 - The bionomial expansi.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&(4+kx)^{5}=\sum_{r=0}^{5}\binom{5}{r}4^{5-r}(kx)^{r}.\\&\text{For }x^{3}\text{ we take }r=3:\\&T_{4}=\binom{5}{3}4^{2}(kx)^{3}=10\cdot16k^{3}x^{3}=160k^{3}x^{3}.\\&\text{Given coefficient of }x^{3}=20:\ 160k^{3}=20\Rightarrow k^{3}=\frac{1}{8}.\\&\therefore k=\frac12.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Smallest angle of a triangle with sides $5,6,10$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 5\text{ cm}$, $BC = 6\text{ cm}$ and $AC = 10\text{ cm}$. Calculate the size of the smallest angle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Identify the smallest side and use the cosine rule on the angle opposite that side: for a triangle with sides $a,b,c$ and opposite angles $A,B,C$, $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos A$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{The smallest side is }AB=5\text{ cm, so the smallest angle is }\angle C\text{ opposite }AB.\\&\text{By the cosine rule in }\triangle ABC:\\&AB^{2}=BC^{2}+AC^{2}-2(BC)(AC)\cos C.\\&5^{2}=6^{2}+10^{2}-2\cdot6\cdot10\cos C\\&25=36+100-120\cos C\\&120\cos C=136-25=111\\&\cos C=\dfrac{111}{120}\approx0.925.\\&C\approx\cos^{-1}(0.925)\approx22^\circ\ (\text{to the nearest degree}).\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Largest angle of a triangle with sides $9.3,6.2,12.7$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 9.3\text{ cm}$, $BC = 6.2\text{ cm}$ and $AC = 12.7\text{ cm}$. Calculate the size of the largest angle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Identify the largest side and use the cosine rule on the angle opposite that side: $a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\cos A$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{Largest side is }AC=12.7\text{ cm, so the largest angle is }\angle B.\\&\text{By the cosine rule:}\\&AC^{2}=AB^{2}+BC^{2}-2(AB)(BC)\cos B.\\&12.7^{2}=9.3^{2}+6.2^{2}-2\cdot9.3\cdot6.2\cos B.\\&161.29=86.49+38.44-115.32\cos B\\&161.29=124.93-115.32\cos B\\&-115.32\cos B=161.29-124.93=36.36\\&\cos B=-\dfrac{36.36}{115.32}\approx-0.315.\\&B\approx\cos^{-1}(-0.315)\approx108^\circ\ (\text{to the nearest degree}).\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Largest angle when sides are in ratio $2:3:4$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: The lengths of the sides of a triangle are in the ratio $2:3:4$. Calculate the size of the largest angle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Let the sides be $2k,3k,4k$. The largest angle is opposite $4k$. Apply the cosine rule: $(4k)^{2}=(2k)^{2}+(3k)^{2}-2(2k)(3k)\cos\theta$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}&\text{Let the sides be }2k,3k,4k,\ \text{largest angle }=\theta\text{ opposite }4k.\\&\text{Cosine rule: }(4k)^{2}=(2k)^{2}+(3k)^{2}-2(2k)(3k)\cos\theta.\\&16k^{2}=4k^{2}+9k^{2}-12k^{2}\cos\theta\\&16k^{2}=13k^{2}-12k^{2}\cos\theta\\&12k^{2}\cos\theta=13k^{2}-16k^{2}=-3k^{2}\\&\cos\theta=-\dfrac{3}{12}=-\dfrac14.\\&\theta\approx\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\dfrac14\right)\approx104^\circ\ (\text{to the nearest degree}).\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Ambiguous case to find $\angle ABC$ and then $AC$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: Triangle $$ABC$$ is such that $$AB = 4\text{ cm}$$, $$BC = 6\text{ cm}$$ and $$\angle ACB = 36^\circ$$. Show that one of the possible values of $$\angle ABC$$ is $$25.8^\circ$$ (to 3 s.f.). Using this value, calculate the length of $$AC$$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with $$AB$$ opposite $$\angle C$$ and $$BC$$ opposite $$\angle A$$ to find two possible values of $$\angle A$$. For each, compute $$\angle B=180^\circ-A-36^\circ$$ and show one is approximately $$25.8^\circ$$. Then, using $$B\approx25.8^\circ$$ and its corresponding $$A$$, apply the sine rule again to find $$AC$$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\text{Sine rule: }\dfrac{AB}{\sin C}=\dfrac{BC}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\dfrac{4}{\sin36^\circ}=\dfrac{6}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\sin A=\dfrac{6\sin36^\circ}{4}=\dfrac32\sin36^\circ\approx\dfrac32\times0.588\approx0.882\Rightarrow A\approx61.9^\circ\text{ or }A'\approx180^\circ-61.9^\circ=118.1^\circ.$$ $$\text{Then }B=180^\circ-36^\circ-61.9^\circ\approx82.1^\circ,\ B'=180^\circ-36^\circ-118.1^\circ\approx25.9^\circ\approx25.8^\circ\text{ (to 3 s.f.), as required. For }B'\approx25.8^\circ\text{ we have }A'\approx118.2^\circ.$$ $$\text{Using this pair in the sine rule, }\dfrac{BC}{\sin A'}=\dfrac{AC}{\sin B'}\Rightarrow\dfrac{6}{\sin118.2^\circ}=\dfrac{AC}{\sin25.8^\circ}\Rightarrow AC=6\dfrac{\sin25.8^\circ}{\sin118.2^\circ}\approx6\dfrac{0.435}{0.881}\approx2.96\text{ cm (to 3 s.f.).}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Largest angles in two possible triangles
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: Two triangles $$ABC$$ are such that $$AB = 4.5\text{ cm}$$, $$BC = 6.8\text{ cm}$$ and $$\angle ACB = 30^\circ$$. Work out the value of the largest angle in each of the triangles.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with $$AB$$ opposite $$\angle C$$ and $$BC$$ opposite $$\angle A$$ to find two possible angles $$A_1$$ and $$A_2=180^\circ-A_1$$. For each triangle compute $$B=180^\circ-A-C$$, then identify, for each case, which of $$A,B,C$$ is largest.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\dfrac{AB}{\sin C}=\dfrac{BC}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\dfrac{4.5}{\sin30^\circ}=\dfrac{6.8}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\dfrac{4.5}{\tfrac12}=\dfrac{6.8}{\sin A}\Rightarrow9=\dfrac{6.8}{\sin A}\Rightarrow\sin A=\dfrac{6.8}{9}\approx0.756.$$ $$\Rightarrow A_1\approx\sin^{-1}(0.756)\approx49.0^\circ,\ A_2\approx180^\circ-49.0^\circ=131.0^\circ.$$ $$\text{For }A_1\approx49.0^\circ,\ B_1=180^\circ-30^\circ-49.0^\circ\approx101.0^\circ,\ \text{so the largest angle is }B_1\approx101^\circ.$$ $$\text{For }A_2\approx131.0^\circ,\ B_2=180^\circ-30^\circ-131.0^\circ\approx19.0^\circ,\ \text{so the largest angle is }A_2\approx131^\circ.$$ $$\text{Thus the largest angles are approximately }101^\circ\text{ and }131^\circ\text{ in the two triangles.}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In a crane arm model, a crane arm $AB$ of length $80\text{ m}$ is anchored at point $B$ at an angle of $40^\circ$ to the horizontal. A wrecking ball is suspended on a cable of length $60\text{ m}$ from $A$. Find the angle $x$ through which the wrecking ball rotates as it passes the two points level with the base of the crane arm at $B$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Drop a perpendicular from $A$ to the horizontal line through $B$ at $H$. Use right-triangle trigonometry to find the vertical height $AH$, then apply $\cos\theta=\dfrac{AH}{AD}$ in triangle $ADH$ where $AD=60\text{ m}$ is the cable and $\theta$ is the angle from the vertical. The total rotation $x$ is $2\theta$ since the motion is symmetric about the vertical.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\text{Let }H\text{ be the foot of the perpendicular from }A\text{ to the horizontal through }B.\ \text{Then }AH=AB\sin40^\circ=80\sin40^\circ.\ \text{When the ball is level with }B,\ \triangle ADH\text{ is right-angled with }AD=60\text{ m and }AH\text{ opposite the horizontal. Let }\angle DAH=\theta.\ \text{Then }\cos\theta=\dfrac{AH}{AD}=\dfrac{80\sin40^\circ}{60}\Rightarrow\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{80\sin40^\circ}{60}\right)\approx31.0^\circ.\ \text{The wrecking ball passes through two symmetric positions on either side of the vertical, so }x=2\theta\approx2\times31.0^\circ\approx62.0^\circ\text{ (to 3 s.f.).}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = (2 - x)\text{ cm}$, $BC = (x + 1)\text{ cm}$ and $\angle ABC = 120^\circ$. a Show that $AC^2 = x^2 - x + 7$. b Find the value of $x$ for which $AC$ has a minimum value.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Apply the cosine rule with the included angle $120^\circ$ to get an expression for $AC^2$ in terms of $x$, then complete the square for $x^2 - x + 7$ to locate the minimum.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned} &\textbf{(a)}\ \text{By the cosine rule with angle at }B: \\ &AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 - 2(AB)(BC)\cos120^\circ. \\ &AB^2 = (2-x)^2 = x^2 - 4x + 4,\quad BC^2 = (x+1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1. \\ &AB\cdot BC = (2-x)(x+1). \\ &\cos120^\circ = -\frac12 \Rightarrow -2(AB)(BC)\cos120^\circ = -2(2-x)(x+1)\left(-\frac12\right) = (2-x)(x+1). \\ &\Rightarrow AC^2 = (x^2 - 4x + 4) + (x^2 + 2x + 1) + (2-x)(x+1). \\ &(2-x)(x+1) = 2x + 2 - x^2 - x = -x^2 + x + 2. \\ &\Rightarrow AC^2 = (x^2 - 4x + 4) + (x^2 + 2x + 1) + (-x^2 + x + 2) \\ &\qquad= x^2 - x + 7,\ \text{as required}. \\ &\textbf{(b)}\ AC^2 = x^2 - x + 7. \text{ Complete the square:} \\ &x^2 - x + 7 = \left(x - \frac12\right)^2 - \left(\frac12\right)^2 + 7 = \left(x - \frac12\right)^2 + \frac{27}{4}. \\ &\left(x - \frac12\right)^2 \ge 0\ \text{for all }x,\ \text{so }AC^2\text{ is minimal when }x - \frac12 = 0. \\ &\Rightarrow x = \frac12. \end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In triangle $ABC$ such that $BC = 5\sqrt2\text{ cm}$, $\angle ABC = 30^\circ$ and $\angle BAC = \theta$, where $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt5}{8}$. Work out the length of $AC$, giving your answer in the form $a\sqrt b$, where $a$ and $b$ are integers.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with side $BC$ opposite $\angle BAC=\theta$ and side $AC$ opposite $\angle ABC=30^\circ$, substituting $\sin\theta=\tfrac{\sqrt5}{8}$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned} &\text{By the sine rule: }\frac{BC}{\sin\angle BAC} = \frac{AC}{\sin\angle ABC}. \\ &\Rightarrow \frac{5\sqrt2}{\sin\theta} = \frac{AC}{\sin30^\circ}. \\ &\sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt5}{8},\ \sin30^\circ = \frac12. \\ &\Rightarrow \frac{5\sqrt2}{\sqrt5/8} = \frac{AC}{1/2}. \\ &\frac{5\sqrt2}{\sqrt5/8} = 5\sqrt2 \cdot \frac{8}{\sqrt5} = \frac{40\sqrt2}{\sqrt5}. \\ &\Rightarrow \frac{40\sqrt2}{\sqrt5} = 2AC \Rightarrow AC = \frac{20\sqrt2}{\sqrt5}. \\ &\text{Rationalise: }\frac{20\sqrt2}{\sqrt5} = 20\sqrt{\frac{2}{5}} = \frac{20\sqrt{10}}{5} = 4\sqrt{10}\text{ cm}. \end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: The perimeter of $\triangle ABC$ is $15\text{ cm}$. Given that $AB = 7\text{ cm}$ and $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$, find the lengths of $AC$ and $BC$ and the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Let $AC = x$ and use the perimeter to write $BC$ in terms of $x$. Then apply the cosine rule with $\angle BAC = 60^\circ$ opposite $BC$ to solve for $x$, and finally use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $AB$ and $AC$ around $\angle BAC$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned} &\text{Let }AC = x\text{ cm}. \text{ Perimeter }AB+BC+AC=15\Rightarrow 7+(8-x)+x=15\Rightarrow BC=8-x\text{ cm}. \\ &\text{Use the cosine rule with angle at }A: \\ &BC^2 = AB^2 + AC^2 - 2(AB)(AC)\cos60^\circ. \\ &(8-x)^2 = 7^2 + x^2 - 2\cdot7\cdot x\cdot\frac12 = 49 + x^2 - 7x. \\ &64 - 16x + x^2 = 49 + x^2 - 7x. \\ &64 - 16x = 49 - 7x \Rightarrow 15 = 9x \Rightarrow x = \frac{15}{9} = \frac53\text{ cm}. \\ &\Rightarrow AC = \frac53\text{ cm},\quad BC = 8 - \frac53 = \frac{24-5}{3} = \frac{19}{3}\text{ cm}. \\ &\text{Area of } \triangle ABC: A = \tfrac12\cdot AB\cdot AC\cdot\sin\angle BAC. \\ &A = \tfrac12\cdot7\cdot\frac53\cdot\sin60^\circ = \frac{35}{6}\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2} = \frac{35\sqrt3}{12}\text{ cm}^2 \approx 5.05\text{ cm}^2. \end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In the triangle $ABC$, $AB = 14\text{ cm}$, $BC = 12\text{ cm}$ and $CA = 15\text{ cm}$. a Find the size of angle $C$, giving your answer to $3$ s.f. b Find the area of triangle $ABC$, giving your answer in cm$^2$ to $3$ s.f.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $AB$ opposite angle $C$ to find $\cos C$ and hence $C$. Then use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $BC$ and $CA$ around angle $C$ to find the area.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned} &\textbf{(a)}\ \text{For angle }C=\angle ACB\text{, the opposite side is }AB=14\text{ cm, with adjacent sides }BC=12\text{ cm and }CA=15\text{ cm}. \\ &\text{Cosine rule: }AB^2 = BC^2 + CA^2 - 2(BC)(CA)\cos C. \\ &14^2 = 12^2 + 15^2 - 2\cdot12\cdot15\cos C. \\ &196 = 144 + 225 - 360\cos C = 369 - 360\cos C. \\ &360\cos C = 369 - 196 = 173 \Rightarrow \cos C = \frac{173}{360} \approx 0.4806. \\ &\Rightarrow C \approx \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{173}{360}\right) \approx 61.3^\circ\ \text{(to 3 s.f.)}. \\ &\textbf{(b)}\ \text{Area }A = \tfrac12\cdot BC\cdot CA\cdot\sin C = \tfrac12\cdot12\cdot15\cdot\sin C = 90\sin C. \\ &\sin C = \sqrt{1-\cos^2 C} = \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{173}{360}\right)^2} \approx 0.876. \\ &\Rightarrow A \approx 90\times0.876 \approx 78.8\text{ cm}^2\ \text{(to 3 s.f.)}. \end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule in $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle BCD$ to get the two angles asked in part (a). Use $\tfrac12ab\sin C$ in each triangle to add their areas for part (b). For part (c), first find the angles at $B$ in $\triangle ABD$ and $\triangle BCD$, add them to get $\angle ABC$, then use the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$ to find $AC$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\textbf{(a)}\ \text{In }\triangle ABD: BD^2=AB^2+AD^2-2(AB)(AD)\cos\angle DAB\Rightarrow5.9^2=4.2^2+2.1^2-2(4.2)(2.1)\cos\angle DAB\Rightarrow\cos\angle DAB=\dfrac{4.2^2+2.1^2-5.9^2}{2\cdot4.2\cdot2.1}\approx-0.723\Rightarrow\angle DAB\approx136^\circ.\ \text{In }\triangle BCD: BD^2=BC^2+CD^2-2(BC)(CD)\cos\angle BCD\Rightarrow5.9^2=7.5^2+3.5^2-2(7.5)(3.5)\cos\angle BCD\Rightarrow\cos\angle BCD=\dfrac{7.5^2+3.5^2-5.9^2}{2\cdot7.5\cdot3.5}\approx0.642\Rightarrow\angle BCD\approx50.1^\circ.$$\ $$\textbf{(b)}\ \text{Area of }\triangle ABD=\tfrac12\cdot AB\cdot AD\sin\angle DAB=\tfrac12\cdot4.2\cdot2.1\sin136^\circ\approx3.04\text{ m}^2.\ \text{Area of }\triangle BCD=\tfrac12\cdot BC\cdot CD\sin\angle BCD=\tfrac12\cdot7.5\cdot3.5\sin50.1^\circ\approx10.1\text{ m}^2.\ \text{Total area}\approx3.04+10.1\approx13.1\text{ m}^2.$$\ $$\textbf{(c)}\ \text{In }\triangle ABD:\ \cos\angle ABD=\dfrac{AB^2+BD^2-AD^2}{2(AB)(BD)}=\dfrac{4.2^2+5.9^2-2.1^2}{2\cdot4.2\cdot5.9}\approx0.969\Rightarrow\angle ABD\approx14.2^\circ.\ \text{In }\triangle BCD:\ \cos\angle CBD=\dfrac{BC^2+BD^2-CD^2}{2(BC)(BD)}=\dfrac{7.5^2+5.9^2-3.5^2}{2\cdot7.5\cdot5.9}\approx0.891\Rightarrow\angle CBD\approx27.1^\circ.\ \Rightarrow\angle ABC=\angle ABD+\angle CBD\approx14.2^\circ+27.1^\circ\approx41.3^\circ.\ \text{Now in }\triangle ABC:\ AC^2=AB^2+BC^2-2(AB)(BC)\cos\angle ABC=4.2^2+7.5^2-2(4.2)(7.5)\cos41.3^\circ\Rightarrow AC\approx5.15\text{ m}.$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.subtopic_name: Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{Sketch the graph of }y=\cos\theta\text{ in the interval }-180^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ.$$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\text{Recall cosine is an even function with period }360^\circ\text{ and amplitude }1.$$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Key properties:}\\\text{Amplitude}&=1\\\text{Period}&=360^\circ\\\text{Even function }&\Rightarrow\text{ symmetric about the }y\text{-axis}\\[6pt]\text{Key points:}\\\theta=-180^\circ&:\ y=\cos(-180^\circ)=-1\\\theta=-90^\circ&:\ y=0\\\theta=0^\circ&:\ y=1\\\theta=90^\circ&:\ y=0\\\theta=180^\circ&:\ y=-1\\[6pt]\text{Plot these points accurately and join them with a smooth cosine curve.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.subtopic_name: Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{Sketch the graph of }y=\tan\theta\text{ in the interval }-180^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ.$$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\text{Recall tangent has period }180^\circ\text{ and vertical asymptotes where }\cos\theta=0.$$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Key properties:}\\\text{Period}&=180^\circ\\\text{Odd function }&\Rightarrow\text{ symmetric about the origin}\\[6pt]\text{Vertical asymptotes:}\\\theta&=-90^\circ,\ 90^\circ\\[6pt]\text{Key points:}\\\theta=-135^\circ&:\ y=\tan(-135^\circ)=1\\\theta=-45^\circ&:\ y=-1\\\theta=0^\circ&:\ y=0\\\theta=45^\circ&:\ y=1\\\theta=135^\circ&:\ y=-1\\[6pt]\text{Draw increasing branches between the asymptotes, passing through the origin.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.subtopic_name: Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{The graph shows the curve }y=\cos(x+30^\circ),\ -360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ.\ \text{(a) Write down the coordinates where the curve crosses the x-axis. (b) Find the coordinates where the curve crosses the y-axis.}$$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\cos\theta=0\text{ at }\theta=90^\circ+180^\circ k;\ \text{y-axis crossing occurs at }x=0.$}$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{(a) x-axis crossings:}\\\cos(x+30^\circ)&=0\\x+30^\circ&=90^\circ+180^\circ k\\x&=60^\circ+180^\circ k\\-360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ\Rightarrow x&=-300^\circ,\ -120^\circ,\ 60^\circ,\ 240^\circ\\\text{Coordinates: }&(-300^\circ,0),(-120^\circ,0),(60^\circ,0),(240^\circ,0)\\[6pt]\textbf{(b) y-axis crossing:}\\x&=0\\y&=\cos(30^\circ)=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\\\text{Coordinate: }&(0,\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.subtopic_name: Graphs of sine, cosine and tangent
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: $$\text{The graph shows }y=\sin(x+k),\ -360^\circ\le x\le360^\circ,\ \text{where }k\text{ is a constant. (a) Find one possible value of }k.\ \text{(b) State whether there is more than one possible value of }k\text{ and give a reason.}$$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: $$\text{Use a key feature such as a maximum or x-axis crossing and compare with }y=\sin x.$}$
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\begin{aligned}\textbf{(a) One possible value of }k:\\\text{From the graph, a maximum occurs at }x&=60^\circ\\\text{For }y=\sin(x+k),\text{ maxima occur when }x+k&=90^\circ\\k&=90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ\\[6pt]\textbf{(b) More than one value?}\\\sin(x+k)\text{ has period }360^\circ&\Rightarrow k=30^\circ+360^\circ n,\ n\in\mathbb{Z}\\\text{So there are infinitely many possible values of }k.\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: Triangle $ABC$ has area $10\text{ cm}^2$. $AB = 6\text{ cm}$, $BC = 8\text{ cm}$ and $\angle ABC$ is obtuse. Find: a the size of $\angle ABC$ b the length of $AC$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ to find $\sin B$ and choose the obtuse angle; then use the cosine rule to find $AC$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $10=\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot8\sin B\Rightarrow10=24\sin B\Rightarrow\sin B=\tfrac{5}{12}\Rightarrow B=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\tfrac{5}{12}\right)\approx24^\circ,\ \text{but }B\text{ is obtuse so }B=180^\circ-24^\circ=156^\circ.\ \text{Next }AC^2=6^2+8^2-2\cdot6\cdot8\cos156^\circ=36+64-96\cos156^\circ,\ \cos156^\circ=-\cos24^\circ\approx-0.9135\Rightarrow AC^2\approx187.7\Rightarrow AC\approx13.7\text{ cm}.$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In triangle $a$, the three sides are $2.4\text{ cm}$, $3\text{ cm}$ and $1.2\text{ cm}$, and angle $x$ is opposite the $2.4\text{ cm}$ side. Find the size of $x$ and the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule to find $x$ from the three sides, then use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with the two sides around $x$ to get the area.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $2.4^2=3^2+1.2^2-2\cdot3\cdot1.2\cos x\Rightarrow\cos x=\dfrac{3^2+1.2^2-2.4^2}{2\cdot3\cdot1.2}=0.65\Rightarrow x\approx\cos^{-1}(0.65)\approx49.5^\circ.\ \text{Area}=\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot1.2\sin x\approx\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot1.2\cdot\sin49.5^\circ\approx1.37\text{ cm}^2.$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In triangle $b$, two sides are $6\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$ and the included angles at the other two vertices are $x^\circ$ and $80^\circ$ as shown. Find the size of $x$ and the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with side $6\text{ cm}$ opposite $80^\circ$ to find the top angle, then use the angle sum of a triangle to get $x$, and finally $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $6$ and $5$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: \text{Let the top angle be }B.\ \dfrac{6}{\sin80^\circ}=\dfrac{5}{\sin B}\Rightarrow\sin B=\dfrac{5\sin80^\circ}{6}\approx0.821\Rightarrow B\approx55.2^\circ.\ \text{Angles in a triangle: }x=180^\circ-80^\circ-B\approx180^\circ-80^\circ-55.2^\circ\approx44.8^\circ.\ \text{Area}=\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot5\sin B\approx\tfrac12\cdot6\cdot5\cdot\sin55.2^\circ\approx12.3\text{ cm}^2.$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In triangle $c$, two sides are $3\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$ and the angle at the end of the $3\text{ cm}$ side is $40^\circ$, with $x^\circ$ the angle between the $3\text{ cm}$ and $5\text{ cm}$ sides. Find the size of $x$ and the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the sine rule with sides $5\text{ cm}$ and $3\text{ cm}$ opposite the other two angles to find the third angle, then use angle sum to get $x$, and finish with $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ using the sides $3$ and $5$ and included angle $x$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: \text{Let the angles opposite }5\text{ cm},3\text{ cm},\text{ and the base be }40^\circ,C,\text{ and }x\text{ respectively. By the sine rule }\dfrac{5}{\sin40^\circ}=\dfrac{3}{\sin C}\Rightarrow\sin C=\dfrac{3\sin40^\circ}{5}\approx0.386\Rightarrow C\approx22.7^\circ.\ \text{Angles in a triangle: }x=180^\circ-40^\circ-C\approx180^\circ-40^\circ-22.7^\circ\approx117.3^\circ.\ \text{Area}=\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot5\sin x\approx\tfrac12\cdot3\cdot5\cdot\sin117.3^\circ\approx6.66\text{ cm}^2.$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Largest angle and area from three sides
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: The sides of a triangle are $3\text{ cm}$, $5\text{ cm}$ and $7\text{ cm}$ respectively. Show that the largest angle is $120^\circ$, and find the area of the triangle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $7\text{ cm}$ opposite the largest angle, then use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $3$ and $5$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$7^2 = 3^2 + 5^2 - 2\cdot3\cdot5\cos C \Rightarrow 49 = 9 + 25 - 30\cos C \Rightarrow 49 = 34 - 30\cos C \Rightarrow 15 = -30\cos C \Rightarrow \cos C = -\tfrac12 \Rightarrow C = 120^\circ.$$ $$\text{Area} = \tfrac12\cdot3\cdot5\sin120^\circ = \tfrac{15}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2} = \tfrac{15\sqrt3}{4}\text{ cm}^2.$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 10\text{ cm}$, $BC = a\sqrt3\text{ cm}$, $AC = 5\sqrt{13}\text{ cm}$ and $\angle ABC = 150^\circ$. Calculate: a the value of $a$ b the exact area of $\triangle ABC$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use the cosine rule with side $AC$ opposite $\angle ABC$ to find $a$, then use $A=\tfrac12 ab\sin C$ with sides $AB$ and $BC$ and angle $150^\circ$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\text{Cosine rule: }(5\sqrt{13})^2 = 10^2 + (a\sqrt3)^2 - 2\cdot10\cdot a\sqrt3\cos150^\circ.$$ $$325 = 100 + 3a^2 - 20a\sqrt3\cdot\left(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right) = 100 + 3a^2 + 30a.$$ $$\Rightarrow 3a^2 + 30a + 100 - 325 = 0 \Rightarrow 3a^2 + 30a - 225 = 0 \Rightarrow a^2 + 10a - 75 = 0.$$ $$a = \frac{-10 \pm \sqrt{10^2 - 4\cdot1\cdot(-75)}}{2} = \frac{-10 \pm 20}{2} \Rightarrow a = 5\ (\text{reject }a=-15).$$ $$BC = 5\sqrt3\text{ cm},\ \text{area} = \tfrac12\cdot10\cdot5\sqrt3\sin150^\circ = \tfrac12\cdot10\cdot5\sqrt3\cdot\tfrac12 = 25\sqrt3\text{ cm}^2.$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: In a triangle, the largest side has length $2\text{ cm}$ and one of the other sides has length $\sqrt2\text{ cm}$. Given that the area of the triangle is $1\text{ cm}^2$, show that the triangle is right-angled and isosceles.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Let the angle between the sides $2$ and $\sqrt2$ be $\theta$. Use the area formula to find $\theta$, then use the cosine rule to find the third side and the angle opposite the largest side.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$1 = \tfrac12\cdot2\cdot\sqrt2\sin\theta \Rightarrow 1 = \sqrt2\sin\theta \Rightarrow \sin\theta = \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}.$$ $$\theta = 45^\circ\ \text{or}\ 135^\circ,\ \text{but if }\theta=135^\circ\text{ the third side would exceed }2\text{ cm, contradicting that }2\text{ is the largest side, so }\theta = 45^\circ.$$ $$\text{Cosine rule for the third side }x:\ x^2 = 2^2 + (\sqrt2)^2 - 2\cdot2\cdot\sqrt2\cos45^\circ = 4 + 2 - 4\sqrt2\cdot\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} = 6 - 4 = 2,$$ $$\Rightarrow x = \sqrt2\text{ cm, so the two smaller sides are both }\sqrt2\text{ cm (isosceles).}$$ $$\text{Angle opposite side }2\text{ (call it }C\text{): } \cos C = \dfrac{\sqrt2^2 + \sqrt2^2 - 2^2}{2\cdot\sqrt2\cdot\sqrt2} = \dfrac{2 + 2 - 4}{4} = 0 \Rightarrow C = 90^\circ.$$ $$\text{Thus the triangle is right-angled and isosceles.}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_title: Cosine of angle and area from coordinates
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: The three points $A$, $B$ and $C$, with coordinates $A(0,1)$, $B(3,4)$ and $C(1,3)$ respectively, are joined to form a triangle. a Show that $\cos\angle ACB = -\dfrac45$. b Calculate the area of $\triangle ABC$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Form vectors $\overrightarrow{CA}$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}$ and use the dot product to find $\cos\angle ACB$, then use the coordinate (determinant) formula for the area of a triangle.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: $$\overrightarrow{CA} = A - C = (-1,-2),\ \overrightarrow{CB} = B - C = (2,1).$$ $$\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{CB} = (-1)(2) + (-2)(1) = -4,\ |\overrightarrow{CA}| = |\overrightarrow{CB}| = \sqrt{(-1)^2 + (-2)^2} = \sqrt5.$$ $$\cos\angle ACB = \dfrac{\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{CB}}{|\overrightarrow{CA}||\overrightarrow{CB}|} = \dfrac{-4}{\sqrt5\cdot\sqrt5} = -\dfrac45.$$ $$\text{Area} = \tfrac12\left|x_A(y_B - y_C) + x_B(y_C - y_A) + x_C(y_A - y_B)\right| = \tfrac12\left|0(4-3) + 3(3-1) + 1(1-4)\right|$$ $$= \tfrac12|0 + 6 - 3| = \tfrac12\cdot3 = \tfrac32\text{ square units.}$$

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: A park is in the shape of a triangle $ABC$ as shown. A park keeper walks due north from his hut at $A$ until he reaches point $B$. He then walks on a bearing of $110^\circ$ to point $C$. a Find how far he is from his hut when at point $C$. Give your answer in km to $3$ s.f. b Work out the bearing of the hut from point $C$. Give your answer to the nearest degree. c Work out the area of the park.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Use bearings to find $\angle ABC=180^\circ-110^\circ$, then apply the cosine rule to get $AC$; use components or triangle angles to get the bearing of $A$ from $C$; use $A=\tfrac12ab\sin C$ for the area.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: In $\triangle ABC$ we have $AB=1.2$, $BC=1.4$ (in km) and $\angle ABC=180^\circ-110^\circ=70^\circ$ since $BA$ has bearing $180^\circ$ and $BC$ has bearing $110^\circ$; by the cosine rule $AC^2=1.2^2+1.4^2-2(1.2)(1.4)\cos70^\circ\approx2.251\Rightarrow AC\approx1.50\text{ km}$, so he is $1.50\text{ km}$ from his hut; to find the bearing of $A$ from $C$, resolve $BC$: from $B$ to $C$ the east component is $1.4\sin110^\circ\approx1.32$ and the north component is $1.4\cos110^\circ\approx-0.48$, so relative to $A$ we have $C$ at $(E,N)\approx(1.32,1.2-0.48)=(1.32,0.72)$; the vector from $C$ to $A$ has components $(-1.32,-0.72)$, so the bearing of $A$ from $C$ is $\theta\approx241^\circ$ (using $\theta=\operatorname{bearing}=\arg(E,N)$); the area of the park is $A=\tfrac12\cdot1.2\cdot1.4\sin70^\circ\approx0.789\text{ km}^2$.

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: A windmill has four identical triangular sails made from wood. If each triangle has sides of length $12\text{ m}$, $15\text{ m}$ and $20\text{ m}$, work out the total area of wood needed.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: First find the area of one triangle using Heron’s formula with semiperimeter $s$, then multiply by $4$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: For one triangle $a=12$, $b=15$, $c=20$; the semiperimeter is $s=\tfrac{12+15+20}{2}=23.5$; by Heron’s formula the area is $\sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}=\sqrt{23.5\times11.5\times8.5\times3.5}\approx89.7\text{ m}^2$; there are $4$ identical sails, so the total area of wood is $4\times89.7\approx359\text{ m}^2$ (to $3$ s.f.).

Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.question_text: Two points, $A$ and $B$ are on level ground. A church tower at point $C$ has an angle of elevation from $A$ of $15^\circ$ and an angle of elevation from $B$ of $32^\circ$. $A$ and $B$ are both on the same side of $C$, and $A$, $B$ and $C$ lie on the same straight line. The distance $AB = 75\text{ m}$. Find the height of the church tower.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.hint: Draw a horizontal line through $A$ and $B$ to the foot of the tower and let the horizontal distance from $B$ to the tower be $x$; use $\tan$ in right-angled triangles from $A$ and $B$ to form two equations in $x$ and the height $h$, then solve for $h$.
Chapter 9 - Trigonometric ratios.correct_answer: Let $x$ be the horizontal distance from $B$ to the foot of the tower and $h$ the height; then from $B$, $\tan32^\circ=\dfrac{h}{x}\Rightarrow h=x\tan32^\circ$; from $A$, the horizontal distance is $x+75$ so $\tan15^\circ=\dfrac{h}{x+75}$; substituting $h$ gives $\tan15^\circ=\dfrac{x\tan32^\circ}{x+75}$ which rearranges to $x\tan32^\circ=\tan15^\circ(x+75)$; solving for $x$ gives $x=\dfrac{75\tan15^\circ}{\tan32^\circ-\tan15^\circ}\approx56.3\text{ m}$; hence $h=x\tan32^\circ\approx56.3\times\tan32^\circ\approx35.2\text{ m}$, so the tower is approximately $35.2\text{ m}$ high.
